pos: n. (the frame or litter on which a corpse is carried out — Hebrew mittah, a bed; Greek soros)
etymology: Old English bær, from the verb to bear — the thing on which a body is borne. The Hebrew word is simply bed; the dead man was carried out on the couch he had lain upon.
biblical_def: A bier is the open frame on which the dead were carried to burial, and Scripture records two of them. At Hebron, David made a nation grieve over a murdered captain: “Rend your clothes, and gird you with sackcloth, and mourn before Abner. And king David himself followed the bier” (2Sa 3:31). The king walked behind the litter of a man who had lately been his enemy, and Israel understood by it that the murder was not of the king's doing. At Nain the Lord Jesus met a very different procession: a widow's only son being carried out of the city gate. “And he came and touched the bier: and they that bare him stood still. And he said, Young man, I say unto thee, Arise” (Luk 7:14). Every detail is deliberate. He touched the bier — contact that made a man ceremonially unclean under the law, and which in His case ran the other way, cleanness passing into the corpse instead of defilement into Him. The bearers stood still, since a procession moving toward a grave has nothing to do when the Lord of life stops it. And He spoke to a dead man as though he could hear, because he could. “And he that was dead sat up, and began to speak. And he delivered him to his mother” (Luk 7:15). Luke notes first what moved Him: “when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her, and said unto her, Weep not” (Luk 7:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a bier as a carriage or frame of wood for conveying dead human bodies to the grave.
webster_full: BIER, n. A carriage or frame of wood for conveying dead human bodies to the grave.
BEAR, v.t. To support; to sustain; to carry; from which the noun bier is formed.
HEARSE, n. A carriage for conveying the dead to the grave; anciently a temporary monument over a grave.
FU'NERAL, n. Burial; the ceremony of burying a dead body; the procession of persons attending the burial.
scriptures: Luke 7:14
And he came and touched the bier: and they that bare him stood still. And he said, Young man, I say unto thee, Arise.
Luke 7:13
And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her, and said unto her, Weep not.
Luke 7:15
And he that was dead sat up, and began to speak. And he delivered him to his mother.
2 Samuel 3:31
And David said to Joab, and to all the people that were with him, Rend your clothes, and gird you with sackcloth, and mourn before Abner. And king David himself followed the bier.
corruption_summary: Death is hidden from view and its rites made pleasant, so that the plain confrontation Scripture stages at the city gate never happens.
corruption_paragraphs: The bier was carried in the open, through the gate, past the whole town, and everyone stopped for it. Modern arrangements do the opposite: the body is removed by professionals, prepared out of sight, and displayed briefly in a room designed to soften what it is. Something is lost with the bier, and it is not merely custom. The public carrying of the dead taught a community what it is and what awaits it, and the Lord chose exactly such a moment to raise a man. Where death is managed rather than faced, the resurrection has nothing to answer, and Christian funerals become gatherings that do everything except look at the coffin and preach the hope.

Luke 7 also fixes the order of Christ's compassion and His power, which is regularly inverted. He saw her — the widow, now childless, with no man left to provide — and had compassion, and only then touched the bier. The miracle served the mercy; the mercy did not decorate the miracle. And when the young man rose, the Lord did not enroll him as a disciple or make an example of him: he delivered him to his mother. That is what the power of Christ is for.
roots_summary: Hebrew mittah (H4296), a bed or couch, used of the bier in 2 Samuel 3:31; Greek soros (G4673), a funeral bier or coffin, Luke 7:14 only.
roots_lines: Hebrew mittah (H4296) — a bed, couch; 2 Samuel 3:31, where the margin reads bed.
Greek soros (G4673) — a funeral urn or bier; Luke 7:14, its only occurrence in the New Testament.
Greek bastazo (G941) — to bear, carry; of the bearers who stood still at His touch.
Old English bær, from beran, to bear — the word names the carrying, not the box.
Numbers 19:11 made touching a corpse defiling; at Nain the touch ran the other way.
usage: “He came and touched the bier” — the defilement ran backwards that day.
“They that bare him stood still” — a funeral halted mid-procession.
“He delivered him to his mother” — what the power was for.

pos: n. (a coop or trap for birds; figuratively, a house full of ill-gotten gain — Hebrew kelub)
etymology: Latin cavea, a hollow or enclosure, through Old French cage. The Hebrew kelub is a basket or fowler's coop, woven of wicker.
biblical_def: A cage in Scripture is a fowler's basket, and both uses of the word are indictments. Jeremiah describes the rich men of Jerusalem: “As a cage is full of birds, so are their houses full of deceit: therefore they are become great, and waxen rich” (Jer 5:27). The picture is precise and ugly — a trapper's coop crammed with birds he took by snaring, and beside it a great house crammed with wealth taken the same way. The next verse names the fruit: “They are waxen fat, they shine: yea, they overpass the deeds of the wicked: they judge not the cause, the cause of the fatherless, yet they prosper; and the right of the needy do they not judge” (Jer 5:28). The prosperity is real; so is the ruin coming. The other use closes the Bible's account of the great city: “Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen, and is become the habitation of devils, and the hold of every foul spirit, and a cage of every unclean and hateful bird” (Rev 18:2). What Jeremiah saw in a merchant's house, John sees as the final state of the whole system — and heaven's command to the saints inside it is immediate: “Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins, and that ye receive not of her plagues” (Rev 18:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a cage as a box or inclosure, made with lattices or open work, for confining birds or beasts; and also a place of confinement for petty criminals.
webster_full: CAGE, n. A box or inclosure, made of boards, or with lattice work of wood, wicker or wire, for confining birds or beasts.
2. A place of confinement for petty criminals.
CAGE, v.t. To confine in a cage; to shut up or confine.
FOWL'ER, n. A sportsman who pursues wild fowls, or takes or kills them for food.
scriptures: Jeremiah 5:27
As a cage is full of birds, so are their houses full of deceit: therefore they are become great, and waxen rich.
Jeremiah 5:28
They are waxen fat, they shine: yea, they overpass the deeds of the wicked: they judge not the cause, the cause of the fatherless, yet they prosper; and the right of the needy do they not judge.
Revelation 18:2

And he cried mightily with a strong voice, saying, Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen, and is become the habitation of devils, and the hold of every foul spirit, and a cage of every unclean and hateful bird.
Revelation 18:4
And I heard another voice from heaven, saying, Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins, and that ye receive not of her plagues.
corruption_summary: Prosperity is read as evidence of God's approval, when Jeremiah shows the same men waxen rich and under sentence for the very means by which they got it.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 5:27-28 is one of the plainest refutations in Scripture of the notion that wealth certifies righteousness. The houses are full, the men are great and rich, they are waxen fat and they shine — and the same paragraph says their houses are full of deceit and that they will not judge the cause of the fatherless. Prosperity proves nothing about a man's standing with God; it only reveals what he does with what he has. The cage full of trapped birds is the prophet's image for how the fortune was made, and God notices the trapping as well as the wealth.

Revelation 18 shows where the system ends and what the church is to do meanwhile. Babylon becomes a cage of every unclean and hateful bird — a place that collects what is foul because that is what it was always gathering — and the voice from heaven does not tell the saints to reform it but to come out of her. The reason given is twofold and exact: that ye be not partakers of her sins, and that ye receive not of her plagues. Participation and judgment travel together. A believer entangled in a system built on deceit will share both its business and its verdict, and the only remedy offered in the text is separation.
roots_summary: Hebrew kelub (H3619), a wicker basket or fowler's cage — Jeremiah 5:27, Amos 8:1; Greek phulake (G5438), a hold, ward, or cage — Revelation 18:2.
roots_lines: Hebrew kelub (H3619) — a basket or cage of wicker; Jeremiah 5:27, and Amos 8:1 of the basket of summer fruit.
Greek phulake (G5438) — a guard, prison, hold; Revelation 18:2, where the same word is rendered hold and cage in one verse.
Latin cavea, a hollow — the enclosure that holds what has been taken.
The image is the fowler's, not the pet-keeper's: birds trapped for profit, not birds kept for pleasure.
Revelation 18:4 gives the only counsel offered to God's people inside such a house: come out.
usage: “As a cage is full of birds, so are their houses full of deceit”.
“They are waxen fat, they shine… yet they prosper” — and are under sentence.
“Come out of her, my people” — separation, not reform.

pos: n. (a private inner room; the place of secret prayer — Greek tameion, a storeroom)
etymology: Old French closet, a small enclosure, from Latin clausum, shut. The Greek tameion is an inner chamber or storeroom — the windowless room at the centre of an eastern house.
biblical_def: The closet is the room where a man prays where no one can see. The Lord's command is explicit: “But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly” (Mat 6:6). The Greek word means an inner storeroom, the most private space in an eastern house, and three actions are commanded in order: enter, shut the door, pray. Each is deliberate. The command comes in a context that names the alternative: “thou shalt not be as the hypocrites are: for they love to pray standing in the synagogues and in the corners of the streets, that they may be seen of men. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward” (Mat 6:5). The hypocrite is not condemned for praying in public — Scripture is full of public prayer — but for praying in order to be seen, and the Lord notes with terrible brevity that he gets exactly what he was after. Nor is length the substitute: “use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do: for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking” (Mat 6:7). Joel uses the word of a bride's chamber in a summons to national repentance so urgent that even the newly married must leave it: “let the bridegroom go forth of his chamber, and the bride out of her closet” (Joe 2:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a closet as a small room or apartment for retirement; any room for privacy; and a place of private devotion.
webster_full: CLOS'ET, n. A small room or apartment for retirement; any room for privacy.
2. An apartment for curiosities or valuable things.
3. A place of private devotion, as in the Scriptures: enter into thy closet.
CLOS'ET, v.t. To shut up in a closet; to conceal; to take into a private apartment for consultation.
scriptures: Matthew 6:6
But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly.
Matthew 6:5

And when thou prayest, thou shalt not be as the hypocrites are: for they love to pray standing in the synagogues and in the corners of the streets, that they may be seen of men. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward.
Matthew 6:7
But when ye pray, use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do: for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking.
Joel 2:16
Gather the people, sanctify the congregation, assemble the elders, gather the children, and those that suck the breasts: let the bridegroom go forth of his chamber, and the bride out of her closet.
corruption_summary: Prayer is made a performance before an audience, or dismissed as unnecessary because God already knows — and the shut door of Matthew 6 answers both.
corruption_paragraphs: The hypocrite's prayer has changed venue but not nature. Where once it stood at the street corner, it now appears wherever prayer can be observed and admired, and the Lord's verdict is the same: they have their reward. The words are colder than they first sound. The reward was the notice of men, the notice was received in full, and the account is closed; nothing further is owed. Against that the closet is prescribed as the ordinary form of a Christian's prayer — not because public prayer is wrong, but because a man who never prays where none can see him has no evidence that he prays to God at all.

The second corruption argues from God's omniscience to prayer's uselessness: He knows what we need, so why ask? The Lord Himself raises the fact and draws the opposite conclusion — your Father knoweth what things ye have need of before ye ask Him, therefore pray after this manner. Prayer is not information supplied to God; it is a son coming to a Father, and the shut door exists so that the son may come without an audience. Joel's use of the word rounds it out: there are moments when even the bride must leave her closet, because the assembly is called and the whole people must fast together. Secret prayer is the rule; corporate solemnity is not its rival.
roots_summary: Greek tameion (G5009), an inner storeroom or private chamber — Matthew 6:6, Luke 12:3, Luke 12:24; Hebrew chuppah (H2646), a canopy or bridal chamber, in Joel 2:16.
roots_lines: Greek tameion (G5009) — an inner chamber, storeroom; Matthew 6:6, Matthew 24:26, Luke 12:3.
Hebrew chuppah (H2646) — a bridal canopy or chamber; Joel 2:16, Psalm 19:5.
Greek battologeo (G945) — to repeat idly, use vain repetitions; Matthew 6:7 only.
The room in view is the windowless inner store of an eastern house — the one place with no spectators.
Three commands in order: enter, shut the door, pray — the shutting is not incidental.
usage: “Enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door” — the door is part of the command.
“They have their reward” — received in full, account closed.
“Thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly”.

pos: n. (a temporary hut or booth in a field; a frail shelter — Hebrew sukkah and melunah)
etymology: From cot, a small hut, Old English cote. The Hebrew words behind it mean a booth of branches and a night-hut — not a cosy dwelling but a watchman's temporary shed.
biblical_def: A cottage in the Authorized Version is not a snug country house but a flimsy watchman's hut thrown up in a field for one season. Isaiah uses it in his first chapter for what was left of Judah after invasion: “And the daughter of Zion is left as a cottage in a vineyard, as a lodge in a garden of cucumbers, as a besieged city” (Isa 1:8). A vineyard booth stands alone in a stripped field after the harvest — the one thing left standing in a landscape that has been taken. That is what remained of Jerusalem, and the next verse says why anything remained at all: “Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom, and we should have been like unto Gomorrah” (Isa 1:9). The word returns in the apocalyptic chapter: “The earth shall reel to and fro like a drunkard, and shall be removed like a cottage; and the transgression thereof shall be heavy upon it; and it shall fall, and not rise again” (Isa 24:20). The whole earth, at the last, will be taken down as easily as a hut of branches. And Isaiah answers the picture with a better shelter: “there shall be a tabernacle for a shadow in the daytime from the heat, and for a place of refuge, and for a covert from storm and from rain” (Isa 4:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a cottage as a small house; a hut; a mean habitation; and notes the scriptural use of a temporary booth or shed erected in a field.
webster_full: COT'TAGE, n. A cot; a hut; a small mean habitation.
2. In the Scriptures, a temporary shed or booth set up in a vineyard or garden, for the keeper during harvest.
LODGE, n. A small house in a park or forest; a temporary habitation; a hut.
BOOTH, n. A house or shed built of boards, boughs of trees, or other slight materials, for a temporary residence.
scriptures: Isaiah 1:8
And the daughter of Zion is left as a cottage in a vineyard, as a lodge in a garden of cucumbers, as a besieged city.
Isaiah 1:9
Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom, and we should have been like unto Gomorrah.
Isaiah 24:20
The earth shall reel to and fro like a drunkard, and shall be removed like a cottage; and the transgression thereof shall be heavy upon it; and it shall fall, and not rise again.
Isaiah 4:6
And there shall be a tabernacle for a shadow in the daytime from the heat, and for a place of refuge, and for a covert from storm and from rain.
corruption_summary: The permanence of the present world is assumed, and the remnant Isaiah calls a bare survival is mistaken for a secure inheritance.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 24:20 says the earth will be removed like a cottage — taken down the way a watchman's booth is dismantled when the harvest is over. Every calculation that treats the present order as the fixed background against which life is planned runs against that sentence. This is not an argument for carelessness about the world; the same Scripture makes men stewards of it. It is an argument against the settled assumption that what is here will remain, an assumption that shapes how men spend, build, and hope without ever being examined.

Isaiah 1:8-9 guards the other flank. The daughter of Zion left as a cottage in a vineyard is not a picture of pleasant simplicity but of catastrophic loss, and the survival of even that much is credited entirely to the LORD of hosts leaving a very small remnant. Where a church reads its own survival as proof of its strength, this verse corrects it. What is left is left by mercy, and the alternative named is Sodom. The chapter that begins with the ruined booth is the same chapter that offers, though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow.
roots_summary: Hebrew sukkah (H5521), a booth of branches — Isaiah 1:8, and the booths of the feast of tabernacles; melunah (H4412), a night-hut, lodge — Isaiah 1:8, 24:20.
roots_lines: Hebrew sukkah (H5521) — a booth, hut of branches; Isaiah 1:8, Leviticus 23:42 of the feast of tabernacles, Jonah 4:5.
Hebrew melunah (H4412) — a night lodge, a hut for a watchman; Isaiah 1:8 and 24:20 only.
Hebrew miqsha (H4750) — a garden of cucumbers; the parallel image in Isaiah 1:8.
The booth is temporary by design: raised for a harvest, taken down after it.
Isaiah 4:6 answers the frail booth with a tabernacle God Himself provides for refuge and covert.
usage: “Left as a cottage in a vineyard” — one hut standing in a stripped field.
“Shall be removed like a cottage” — the earth taken down after harvest.
“Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant” — the survival is mercy.

pos: n. pl. (papyrus reeds of the Nile, woven into baskets and boats — Hebrew gome)
etymology: From bull (in the old sense of large or coarse) and rush. The Hebrew gome is the papyrus, the reed of Egypt from which baskets, boats and writing material were made.
biblical_def: Bulrushes are the papyrus reeds of the Nile, and the Authorized Version uses the word at the hinge of Israel's deliverance. Pharaoh had commanded that every Hebrew son be cast into the river. Jochebed obeyed the letter of the decree and defeated it: “when she could not longer hide him, she took for him an ark of bulrushes, and daubed it with slime and with pitch, and put the child therein; and she laid it in the flags by the river's brink” (Exo 2:3). The word for the little vessel is ark — the same word used of Noah's, and used nowhere else in Scripture. Both arks were daubed with pitch, both carried a deliverer through waters of judgment, and both were built by a believer acting on a word from God. Pharaoh's daughter came down to wash: “when she saw the ark among the flags, she sent her maid to fetch it” (Exo 2:5), and “when she had opened it, she saw the child: and, behold, the babe wept. And she had compassion on him, and said, This is one of the Hebrews' children” (Exo 2:6). Isaiah uses the same reed of Ethiopian diplomacy: a nation “that sendeth ambassadors by the sea, even in vessels of bulrushes upon the waters” (Isa 18:2). Empires travel in papyrus boats; so did the man who broke one.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a bulrush as a large kind of rush, growing in wet land or water, of which the ancients made baskets and small vessels; the papyrus of the Nile.
webster_full: BULRUSH, n. A large kind of rush, growing in wet land or water, and without knots.
2. The papyrus of Egypt, of which the ancients made baskets, boats and paper.
ARK, n. A small close vessel, chest or coffer; also the vessel in which Noah and his family were preserved, and that in which Moses was set among the flags.
SLIME, n. Soft moist earth having an adhesive quality; bitumen, as used for mortar and for daubing.
scriptures: Exodus 2:3
And when she could not longer hide him, she took for him an ark of bulrushes, and daubed it with slime and with pitch, and put the child therein; and she laid it in the flags by the river's brink.
Exodus 2:5
And the daughter of Pharaoh came down to wash herself at the river; and her maidens walked along by the river's side; and when she saw the ark among the flags, she sent her maid to fetch it.
Exodus 2:6
And when she had opened it, she saw the child: and, behold, the babe wept. And she had compassion on him, and said, This is one of the Hebrews' children.
Isaiah 18:2

That sendeth ambassadors by the sea, even in vessels of bulrushes upon the waters, saying, Go, ye swift messengers, to a nation scattered and peeled, to a people terrible from their beginning hitherto; a nation meted out and trodden down, whose land the rivers have spoiled!
corruption_summary: The account is treated as a folk tale of an exposed infant, and the faith Hebrews credits to Moses' parents is emptied into maternal instinct.
corruption_paragraphs: Critical scholarship has long assimilated Exodus 2 to the ancient pattern of the exposed royal infant, and treated the ark of bulrushes as a legendary motif borrowed and retold. Hebrews 11:23 reads it otherwise and says why: by faith Moses, when he was born, was hid three months of his parents, because they saw he was a proper child; and they were not afraid of the king's commandment. That is a historical claim about the motives of two named people, and it makes the basket an act of faith and civil disobedience rather than a literary convention. Scripture's own commentary on its own narrative is the authoritative one.

The second thing the passage will not surrender is the sovereignty running through it. Pharaoh commanded the river; the river carried the deliverer to Pharaoh's own daughter, who paid the child's mother to nurse him and raised him in the palace of the man who meant to kill him. Every step of the rescue used the machinery of the persecution. This is not fate and not coincidence; it is the God who works all things after the counsel of His own will, and the ark of bulrushes is the small vessel in which He carried a nation's deliverance past a tyrant's decree.
roots_summary: Hebrew gome (H1573), papyrus, the bulrush of the Nile — Exodus 2:3, Isaiah 18:2, Isaiah 35:7, Job 8:11; tebah (H8392), the ark, used only of Noah's vessel and this one.
roots_lines: Hebrew gome (H1573) — papyrus, bulrush; Exodus 2:3, Job 8:11, Isaiah 18:2 and 35:7.
Hebrew tebah (H8392) — ark, chest; used in Scripture only of Noah's ark and the ark of bulrushes.
Hebrew chemar (H2564) and zepheth (H2203) — slime and pitch; the same daubing that sealed Noah's ark.
Hebrew suph (H5488) — flags, reeds; the same word as in the Red Sea, yam suph.
The choice of tebah rather than the ordinary word for basket is deliberate: two arks, two deliverances through water.
usage: “An ark of bulrushes… daubed with slime and with pitch” — the second ark in Scripture.
“She laid it in the flags by the river's brink” — obedience to the decree that defeated it.
“Vessels of bulrushes upon the waters” — empires travelled in the same reed.

pos: n. (a precious sea-growth traded as a jewel — Hebrew ramoth)
etymology: Greek korallion, through Latin corallium. The Hebrew ramoth is rendered coral, and the margin of Job 28:18 preserves the untranslated form.
biblical_def: Coral appears twice in the Authorized Version, both times among the costliest goods of the ancient world. Job's great poem on wisdom lists what cannot buy it: “No mention shall be made of coral, or of pearls: for the price of wisdom is above rubies” (Job 28:18). The whole chapter is built to make one point — men mine silver, cut shafts in the rock, and bring hidden things to light, and after all their searching the question remains: “But where shall wisdom be found? and where is the place of understanding?” (Job 28:12). The answer, at the end of the chapter, is that God alone knows the way to it, and that to man He has said, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom. Ezekiel places coral in the merchandise of Tyre: “Syria was thy merchant by reason of the multitude of the wares of thy making: they occupied in thy fairs with emeralds, purple, and broidered work, and fine linen, and coral, and agate” (Eze 27:16). Tyre's catalogue is deliberately magnificent and deliberately doomed; the chapter ends with the ship sunk. Solomon has already set the valuation the believer is to hold: wisdom “is more precious than rubies: and all the things thou canst desire are not to be compared unto her” (Pro 3:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines coral as a hard substance growing in the sea, formerly ranked among marine plants, of a bright red or white color, much used for ornaments.
webster_full: COR'AL, n. A hard, cretaceous, marine production, formerly supposed to be a plant, of a bright red or white color.
2. A piece of coral worn as an ornament, or given to children.
COR'ALLINE, a. Consisting of coral; like coral; containing coral.
RU'BY, n. A precious stone of a carmine red color, sometimes verging to violet; one of the most valuable of gems.
scriptures: No mention shall be made of coral, or of pearls: for the price of wisdom is above rubies.
But where shall wisdom be found? and where is the place of understanding?
Ezekiel 27:16
Syria was thy merchant by reason of the multitude of the wares of thy making: they occupied in thy fairs with emeralds, purple, and broidered work, and fine linen, and coral, and agate.
Proverbs 3:15
She is more precious than rubies: and all the things thou canst desire are not to be compared unto her.
corruption_summary: Knowledge and information are mistaken for wisdom, so that a generation with unprecedented access to facts has no more of the thing Job says money cannot buy.
corruption_paragraphs: Job 28 is the ancient world's account of technology, and it is admiring: men bind the floods, cut rivers among the rocks, put forth their hand upon the flinty rock, and every precious thing is seen by their eye. Then the question — but where shall wisdom be found? — and the whole apparatus falls silent. That structure is exactly as pointed now. The reach of what men can find out has multiplied beyond anything the chapter imagined, and the multiplication has not produced one grain of the thing in question, because wisdom is not further down the same shaft. It is in the fear of the LORD, and it is given, not mined.

Ezekiel 27 adds the commercial warning. Tyre's inventory — emeralds, purple, broidered work, fine linen, coral, agate — is a catalogue of everything the world calls valuable, listed by a prophet in order to sink it. The chapter closes with merchants hissing at her ruin. That is not an argument against trade, which Scripture regulates rather than forbids; it is a statement about where such an inventory ends when the city that holds it has said, I am a god, I sit in the seat of God. Coral is worth what it is worth. It simply cannot be exchanged for the one thing a man most needs.
roots_summary: Hebrew ramoth (H7215), coral — Job 28:18 and Ezekiel 27:16 only; peninim (H6443), rubies or pearls, the standard of comparison in Proverbs.
roots_lines: Hebrew ramoth (H7215) — coral; Job 28:18 and Ezekiel 27:16, its only occurrences, with the margin keeping Ramoth.
Hebrew peninim (H6443) — rubies, pearls; Job 28:18, Proverbs 3:15, 8:11, 31:10 of the virtuous woman.
Hebrew chokmah (H2451) — wisdom; the subject of Job 28 and the thing no cargo can buy.
Job 28 is structured as a mining expedition that fails: everything precious is found, and wisdom is not.
Ezekiel lists coral among Tyre's wares in a chapter written to sink the ship that carried them.
usage: “No mention shall be made of coral, or of pearls” — the price of wisdom is above them.
“Where shall wisdom be found?” — asked after every shaft has been sunk.
“All the things thou canst desire are not to be compared unto her”.

pos: n. (the older spelling of sponge; the vessel that carried vinegar to the cross — Greek spongos)
etymology: Greek spongos, through Latin spongia. Spunge is the seventeenth-century English spelling retained in the Authorized Version.
biblical_def: The spunge appears in Scripture at one place only: the cross. All three accounts record it. “And straightway one of them ran, and took a spunge, and filled it with vinegar, and put it on a reed, and gave him to drink” (Mat 27:48). Mark adds the crowd's remark: “And one ran and filled a spunge full of vinegar, and put it on a reed, and gave him to drink, saying, Let alone; let us see whether Elias will come to take him down” (Mar 15:36). John supplies the detail that ties it to the Passover: “Now there was set a vessel full of vinegar: and they filled a spunge with vinegar, and put it upon hyssop, and put it to his mouth” (Joh 19:29). Hyssop is the plant with which the blood of the paschal lamb was struck on the door posts in Egypt, and it is hyssop that lifts the drink to the true Lamb as He dies. This drink is not the earlier one He refused. He would not take the wine mingled with myrrh that dulled pain; He received this, because a scripture waited to be fulfilled and a work waited to be finished: “When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost” (Joh 19:30). The last thing to touch the Saviour's lips was sour wine on a sponge, lifted by an enemy's hand.

webster_full: SPUNGE, SPONGE, n. A soft porous substance, found in the sea, remarkable for its property of imbibing water and other fluids.
2. Anything spongy, or that sucks up liquids.
VIN'EGAR, n. Sour wine; a sour liquor obtained by the acetous fermentation of wine, cider or other liquors.
HYS'SOP, n. A plant of the genus Hyssopus, used in the Levitical purifications and in the sprinkling of blood.
scriptures: Matthew 27:48
And straightway one of them ran, and took a spunge, and filled it with vinegar, and put it on a reed, and gave him to drink.
Mark 15:36
And one ran and filled a spunge full of vinegar, and put it on a reed, and gave him to drink, saying, Let alone; let us see whether Elias will come to take him down.
John 19:29
Now there was set a vessel full of vinegar: and they filled a spunge with vinegar, and put it upon hyssop, and put it to his mouth.
John 19:30
When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost.
corruption_summary: The cross is presented as something done to Christ, when the Gospels present a dying Man in command of the sequence, receiving what He chose to receive and finishing what He came to finish.
corruption_paragraphs: The sponge is a small proof of a large doctrine. Christ refused one drink and received another, and the difference was not comfort but purpose: the myrrhed wine would have dulled Him, this vinegar fulfilled a scripture, and the moment He received it He announced the work complete and dismissed His spirit. Every account of Calvary as a tragedy that overtook a good man collapses at this detail. He said, no man taketh my life from me, but I lay it down of myself, and the Gospels record Him doing precisely that, down to the timing of a drink.

John's hyssop deserves the weight he gives it. The plant that struck the lamb's blood on the lintels in Egypt, and that David asked to be purged with, lifts the last drink to the Lamb of God at the hour the Passover lambs were being killed. This is not literary decoration; it is the same God ordering the type and the fulfilment. Where the Old Testament is read as a separate religion superseded rather than a promise kept, the hyssop is invisible, and the reader loses the Bible's own way of showing that one purpose runs from Egypt to Golgotha.

pos: n. pl. (small ornaments of gold worn on the person; not writing tablets — Hebrew kumaz and bath nephesh)
etymology: Diminutive of table, a flat plate, Latin tabula. In the Authorized Version the word does not mean a writing tablet but a small worn ornament — the Hebrew of Isaiah 3:20 means literally houses of the soul, scent-cases worn at the breast.
biblical_def: Tablets in the Authorized Version are jewels, not writing surfaces, and the word appears in three places that between them tell a whole story about ornament. First, at the tabernacle, when the people brought their gold for the sanctuary: “they came, both men and women, as many as were willing hearted, and brought bracelets, and earrings, and rings, and tablets, all jewels of gold: and every man that offered offered an offering of gold unto the LORD” (Exo 35:22). Second, after the battle with Midian, when the captains found not one man missing and brought their spoil: “We have therefore brought an oblation for the LORD, what every man hath gotten, of jewels of gold, chains, and bracelets, rings, earrings, and tablets, to make an atonement for our souls before the LORD” (Num 31:50). Third, in Isaiah's inventory of the finery of the daughters of Zion, which God is about to take away: “The bonnets, and the ornaments of the legs, and the headbands, and the tablets, and the earrings” (Isa 3:20). The same jewels appear in all three, and the difference is entirely in the wearer. Freely offered to God, tablets build a sanctuary and are named as an atonement-offering; worn by a people described as haughty, walking and mincing as they go (Isa 3:16), the identical ornaments are stripped away in judgment.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a tablet as a small flat surface; a medicine in a flat cake or lozenge; and, in the Scriptures, a small ornament of gold worn upon the person.
webster_full: TAB'LET, n. A small table or flat surface.
2. Something flat on which to write, paint or engrave.
3. A small ornament worn on the person; in the Scriptures, jewels of gold offered by the people.
OR'NAMENT, n. That which embellishes; something which, added to another thing, renders it more beautiful to the eye.
scriptures: Exodus 35:22

And they came, both men and women, as many as were willing hearted, and brought bracelets, and earrings, and rings, and tablets, all jewels of gold: and every man that offered offered an offering of gold unto the LORD.
Numbers 31:50

We have therefore brought an oblation for the LORD, what every man hath gotten, of jewels of gold, chains, and bracelets, rings, earrings, and tablets, to make an atonement for our souls before the LORD.
Isaiah 3:20
The bonnets, and the ornaments of the legs, and the headbands, and the tablets, and the earrings,
Isaiah 3:16
Moreover the LORD saith, Because the daughters of Zion are haughty, and walk with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes, walking and mincing as they go, and making a tinkling with their feet:
corruption_summary: Ornament is treated either as sin in itself or as a matter God takes no interest in, and Scripture does neither.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors have long divided the church on this small subject. The first forbids ornament outright and reads Isaiah 3 as a prohibition of jewellery. But the same items, item for item, are brought willingly to the LORD in Exodus 35 and offered as an atonement in Numbers 31, and God receives them and builds His house with them. The gold is not the offence. The second error says appearance is a private matter of no spiritual weight, which Isaiah 3:16 flatly denies: the LORD begins His indictment with how the daughters of Zion walked, and what their eyes and their feet were saying. Manner and adornment are speech, and God hears them.

The distinguishing question in all three passages is the heart behind the ornament. In Exodus the phrase is as many as were willing hearted; in Numbers the soldiers give because not one of their men was missing and they knew who had kept them; in Isaiah the wearers are haughty, with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes. The identical gold serves worship, thanksgiving, or vanity depending entirely on what is under it, and Peter's rule follows the same line — not the outward adorning, but the hidden man of the heart, which is in the sight of God of great price.
roots_summary: Hebrew kumaz (H3558), a jewel or trinket of gold — Exodus 35:22, Numbers 31:50; bath nephesh, literally houses of the soul, scent-bottles or amulets worn at the breast — Isaiah 3:20.

pos: n. pl. (dealers who exchanged coin for the temple tax, at a profit — Greek kollubistai)
etymology: A compound rendering Greek kollubistes, from kollubos, the small coin taken as the fee for exchange. The trade was the changing of foreign currency into the shekel required by the temple.
biblical_def: The moneychangers sat in the court of the Gentiles, exchanging the coinage pilgrims carried into the shekel the temple would accept, and taking a fee on every transaction. The Lord Jesus threw them out. “And Jesus went into the temple of God, and cast out all them that sold and bought in the temple, and overthrew the tables of the moneychangers, and the seats of them that sold doves” (Mat 21:12); Mark records the same at the last Passover (Mar 11:15). His stated ground is a text: “It is written, My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves” (Mat 21:13). The quotation is from Isaiah, and the full sentence there reads a house of prayer for all people — which matters, because the market was set up in the one court where Gentiles were permitted to pray. The trade did not merely dirty the temple; it occupied the only ground the nations had. At the first cleansing John records a different word: “Take these things hence; make not my Father's house an house of merchandise” (Joh 2:16). The service being sold was necessary — pilgrims did need the right coin, and doves were the poor man's offering. What the Lord overturned was the turning of access to God into a trade.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a money-changer as a broker who deals in money, or exchanges coin of one country or denomination for that of another, for a premium.
webster_full: MONEY-CHANGER, n. A broker who deals in money or exchanges.
CHANGE, v.t. To exchange; to give one thing or commodity for another.
MER'CHANDISE, n. The objects of commerce; wares, goods, commodities; whatever is usually bought or sold in trade.
TEM'PLE, n. A public edifice erected in honor of some deity; among Christians, a church.
scriptures: Matthew 21:12
And Jesus went into the temple of God, and cast out all them that sold and bought in the temple, and overthrew the tables of the moneychangers, and the seats of them that sold doves,
Mark 11:15

And they come to Jerusalem: and Jesus went into the temple, and began to cast out them that sold and bought in the temple, and overthrew the tables of the moneychangers, and the seats of them that sold doves;
Matthew 21:13
And said unto them, It is written, My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves.
John 2:16
And said unto them that sold doves, Take these things hence; make not my Father's house an house of merchandise.
corruption_summary: Access to God is sold, and the cleansing of the temple is used to justify every kind of anger except the one it actually addresses.
corruption_paragraphs: The trade the Lord overturned has never stopped. Rome sold indulgences, and the Reformation began over the sale; modern versions sell prayers, anointings, prophecies, and blessings, and the transaction is the same one — a fee levied at the door of God's house. The mark of the sin is not that money changes hands in religion; the temple ran on offerings and Paul says they that preach the gospel should live of the gospel. The mark is that something God gives freely is put behind a price, so that the poor are charged for what was theirs by grace. It is significant that the seats overturned included those of them that sold doves, the offering of the poorest.

The passage is also regularly enlisted for purposes it does not serve. The cleansing is cited to license anger in general, as though the Lord's zeal underwrote every believer's indignation. But the anger here is His, in His own house, over a specific defilement, and grounded in a written text He quoted. Note also whose ground was being occupied: the market stood in the court of the Gentiles, the only place the nations could pray, and Mark records the fuller quotation — a house of prayer for all nations. What was stolen was not merely reverence but the access of the outsider, and that is a sin the modern church can commit without a single coin changing hands.

pos: n. pl. (storehouses for wine and oil under royal charge — Hebrew otsar, a treasury)
etymology: Latin cellarium, a storeroom, from cella, a small chamber. The Hebrew word rendered cellars is the ordinary word for treasury or store.
biblical_def: Cellars occur in the Authorized Version in one passage: the roll of David's stewards at the end of Chronicles' account of his reign. “And over the vineyards was Shimei the Ramathite: over the increase of the vineyards for the wine cellars was Zabdi the Shiphmite” (1Ch 27:27), and “over the olive trees and the sycomore trees that were in the low plains was Baalhanan the Gederite: and over the cellars of oil was Joash” (1Ch 27:28). The list is long and unglamorous — men set over herds, camels, asses, flocks, fields, vineyards, olives, wine and oil, each named with his town. Scripture bothers to record it, and the fact is instructive. A kingdom is administered, and God permits the register of its storerooms into holy writ alongside the psalms of its king. Two chapters later David gathers the whole and gives it away for the house of God, praying, “who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly after this sort? for all things come of thee, and of thine own have we given thee” (1Ch 29:14). That is the theology of the cellars. The store existed, it was carefully kept by named men, and the king who owned it confessed it was never his. The ordinary rule for every believer follows the same shape: “Honour the LORD with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase” (Pro 3:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a cellar as a room under a building, used as a repository of liquors, provisions and other stores for a family.
webster_full: CEL'LAR, n. A room under a building, and usually under ground, used as a repository of liquors, provisions and other stores for a family.
CEL'LARAGE, n. The room or space for cellars; cellars in general.
STORE, n. A large number or quantity; a stock provided; provisions accumulated.
STEW'ARD, n. A man employed in great families to manage the domestic concerns and superintend the other servants.

And over the vineyards was Shimei the Ramathite: over the increase of the vineyards for the wine cellars was Zabdi the Shiphmite:
1 Chronicles 27:28
And over the olive trees and the sycomore trees that were in the low plains was Baalhanan the Gederite: and over the cellars of oil was Joash:
1 Chronicles 29:14
But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly after this sort? for all things come of thee, and of thine own have we given thee.
Proverbs 3:9
Honour the LORD with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase:
corruption_summary: Administration and ownership are confused, so that the man who keeps the store forgets he is a steward, and the man who dislikes stores despises the keeping of them.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is stewardship as an actual occupation. Scripture names the men who kept David's wine and oil, town by town, and preserves their names next to the psalms. Ordinary competent administration — counting, storing, keeping, handing on — is a service God notices and records, and a church that honours only the visible ministries has lost something the Chronicler thought worth writing down.

The temptation of the storehouse is named elsewhere in Scripture and is worth setting beside this list. The rich fool pulled down his barns to build greater and said to his soul, take thine ease; God called him a fool that night. The difference between his barns and David's cellars is not the size of the store but the sentence spoken over it. David's was, of thine own have we given thee. Where that sentence is not said, a full cellar becomes the ground of a false security, and the fuller it is the deeper the lie.

pos: n. (a tree of the well-watered plain, probably the plane — Hebrew armon)
etymology: The older English spelling of chestnut, retained in the Authorized Version. The Hebrew armon is a smooth-barked tree of watercourses, understood by many as the plane tree.
biblical_def: The chesnut appears twice. In Jacob's dealings with Laban: “And Jacob took him rods of green poplar, and of the hazel and chesnut tree; and pilled white strakes in them, and made the white appear which was in the rods” (Gen 30:37). The passage records what Jacob did; the increase that followed is credited elsewhere not to the rods but to God, who told Jacob in a dream that He had seen all that Laban did to him. In Ezekiel the tree stands in a great parable of pride: Assyria is a cedar in Lebanon, and “the cedars in the garden of God could not hide him: the fir trees were not like his boughs, and the chesnut trees were not like his branches; nor any tree in the garden of God was like unto him in his beauty” (Eze 31:8). God Himself takes credit for the height: “I have made him fair by the multitude of his branches: so that all the trees of Eden, that were in the garden of God, envied him” (Eze 31:9). The chapter then cuts him down, because his heart was lifted up in his height. Set against that stands the only tree Scripture promises will not fail: the man who delights in the law of the LORD “shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither” (Psa 1:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the chesnut as a tree of the genus Fagus, and its nut; the Scripture chesnut is understood by many to be the plane tree, which grows by watercourses.
webster_full: CHES'NUT, n. The fruit, seed or nut of a tree of the genus Fagus.
2. The tree itself, valued for its timber and its fruit.
CHES'NUT, a. Being of the color of a chesnut; of a brown color.
PLANE-TREE, n. A tree of the genus Platanus, growing by streams, with a smooth bark which peels off in flakes.
scriptures: Genesis 30:37
And Jacob took him rods of green poplar, and of the hazel and chesnut tree; and pilled white strakes in them, and made the white appear which was in the rods.
Ezekiel 31:8

The cedars in the garden of God could not hide him: the fir trees were not like his boughs, and the chesnut trees were not like his branches; nor any tree in the garden of God was like unto him in his beauty.
Ezekiel 31:9
I have made him fair by the multitude of his branches: so that all the trees of Eden, that were in the garden of God, envied him.
Psalm 1:3
And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper.
corruption_summary: Greatness is read as self-made, when Ezekiel has God saying of the tallest tree in the garden, I have made him fair.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the doctrine Ezekiel 31 states about every eminence: I have made him fair by the multitude of his branches. The greatest empire of its day was tall because God made it tall, and it was cut down because its heart was lifted up in its height. Every account of national or personal greatness that omits the first clause will be unable to explain the second, and will treat the felling as misfortune rather than judgment.

Genesis 30 is worth a second look for a related reason. Jacob's rods of poplar, hazel and chesnut have been read for centuries as either folk superstition or clever animal husbandry, and both readings miss what the narrative itself supplies. Jacob later tells his wives that the angel of God spoke to him in a dream and showed him the cattle, and that God had taken away the cattle of their father and given them to him. The rods are recorded; the increase is attributed. Scripture regularly relates what a man did and then tells us who did it.

pos: n. (a skilled workman; in Scripture, chiefly the maker of idols — Hebrew charash)
etymology: From craft, Old English cræft, skill or power, and man. The Hebrew charash covers the worker in wood, stone or metal — the artificer.
biblical_def: Craftsman in the Authorized Version falls under a curse and under a judgment, and in both cases because of what the skill was used to make. At Ebal the Levites pronounced twelve curses, and the first was this: “Cursed be the man that maketh any graven or molten image, an abomination unto the LORD, the work of the hands of the craftsman, and putteth it in a secret place. And all the people shall answer and say, Amen” (Deu 27:15). The phrase the work of the hands of the craftsman is the indictment: the idol is skilled work, competently done, and that is precisely the problem. Isaiah mocks the process — “The workman melteth a graven image, and the goldsmith spreadeth it over with gold, and casteth silver chains” (Isa 40:19) — and the Psalmist states the conclusion: “Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands” (Psa 115:4). At the end of Scripture the craftsman is silenced with the city he served: “no craftsman, of whatsoever craft he be, shall be found any more in thee; and the sound of a millstone shall be heard no more at all in thee” (Rev 18:22). Yet Scripture does not despise the craft. God Himself filled Bezaleel with the Spirit in wisdom and in all manner of workmanship to build the tabernacle. Skill is a gift; the question is always whose house it builds.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a craftsman as an artificer; a mechanic; one skilled in a manual occupation; and craft as art, skill, dexterity in a manual occupation.
webster_full: CRAFTSMAN, n. An artificer; a mechanic; one skilled in a manual occupation.
CRAFT, n. Art; ability; dexterity; skill; in a good sense, manual art or trade.
2. Cunning, art or skill, in a bad sense; artifice; guile.
AR'TIFICER, n. An artist; a mechanic or manufacturer; one whose occupation requires skill or knowledge of a particular kind.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 27:15

Cursed be the man that maketh any graven or molten image, an abomination unto the LORD, the work of the hands of the craftsman, and putteth it in a secret place. And all the people shall answer and say, Amen.
Isaiah 40:19
The workman melteth a graven image, and the goldsmith spreadeth it over with gold, and casteth silver chains.
Psalm 115:4
Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands.
Revelation 18:22

And the voice of harpers, and musicians, and of pipers, and trumpeters, shall be heard no more at all in thee; and no craftsman, of whatsoever craft he be, shall be found any more in thee; and the sound of a millstone shall be heard no more at all in thee;
corruption_summary: Skill is treated as its own justification, so that excellence in the making is thought to settle the question of what is made.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 27:15 curses an idol precisely as the work of the hands of the craftsman. The image was well made; the maker was good at his trade; and the whole nation was to say Amen to the curse upon it. This cuts against a deep instinct, in the arts and in the trades alike, that craftsmanship is self-justifying — that a thing done superbly has thereby answered for itself. Scripture never grants it. Skill is a gift of God, and a gift can be turned against the Giver with more efficiency than clumsiness ever manages.

The last clause of the curse deserves notice: and putteth it in a secret place. The idol was not paraded; it was hidden. Deuteronomy anticipates the respectable man who keeps the public covenant and keeps a private image too, and it puts the whole congregation on record against him with an Amen. That is the shape of most idolatry in a professing church — not open apostasy but a well-made thing kept in a secret place, and the corrective is the same: name it, and let the man who owns it hear the whole assembly agree that it is accursed.

Against all this stands Exodus 31, where God fills Bezaleel with His Spirit in wisdom, understanding, knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship, to devise cunning works in gold, silver and brass. The craftsman is not the villain of Scripture. Revelation 18 silences him only because the city he served is falling, and the millstone stops with him. A trade offered to God builds a tabernacle; the identical trade offered elsewhere builds an abomination, and nothing in the quality of the work distinguishes them.

pos: n. (a lodging room made ready for a guest; the room of the Last Supper — Greek kataluma)
etymology: From guest, Old Norse gestr, and chamber, Latin camera. The Greek kataluma is a place of unloading — where a traveller loosed his burdens for the night.
biblical_def: The guestchamber is the room in which the Lord kept His last Passover and instituted the Supper. He sent two disciples with a sign and a message: “wheresoever he shall go in, say ye to the goodman of the house, The Master saith, Where is the guestchamber, where I shall eat the passover with my disciples?” (Mar 14:14), and Luke records the same words (Luk 22:11). The answer came as He said it would: “he will shew you a large upper room furnished and prepared: there make ready for us” (Mar 14:15); “he shall shew you a large upper room furnished: there make ready” (Luk 22:12). Two things stand out. First, the Lord speaks of the room as though it were already His — the guestchamber, not a room, and the message is a summons, not a request. Second, the same Greek word is used of the inn at Bethlehem where there was no room for Him. He who was refused a kataluma at His birth claims one at His death. The householder is never named. He had prepared a large upper room, furnished and ready, and the greatest meal in the history of the world was eaten in it. Scripture does not tell us who he was, which is itself a mercy to every believer who serves without a name attached.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a guest-chamber as an apartment appropriated to the entertainment of guests; and a guest as a stranger or friend entertained in the house of another.
webster_full: GUEST-CHAMBER, n. An apartment appropriated to the entertainment of guests.
GUEST, n. A stranger or friend entertained in the house or at the table of another.
CHAM'BER, n. An apartment in an upper story, or in a story above the lower floor of a dwelling house.
GOOD'MAN, n. The master of a house or family; a familiar appellation of civility.
scriptures: Mark 14:14
And wheresoever he shall go in, say ye to the goodman of the house, The Master saith, Where is the guestchamber, where I shall eat the passover with my disciples?
Luke 22:11
And ye shall say unto the goodman of the house, The Master saith unto thee, Where is the guestchamber, where I shall eat the passover with my disciples?
Mark 14:15
And he will shew you a large upper room furnished and prepared: there make ready for us.
Luke 22:12
And he shall shew you a large upper room furnished: there make ready.
corruption_summary: The Supper is detached from the room and the household that housed it, and Christian hospitality is reduced to entertaining rather than the ordinary service by which the church has always been sheltered.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the plain, unnamed service of the goodman of the house. He had a large upper room furnished and prepared, and when the message came — the Master saith — it was available. Scripture records the room in three Gospels and never records his name. Every congregation depends on such people, and every believer with a house has a version of the question: is the room prepared, and would it be given if the Master sent for it?

There is a second point in the wording that the church should not lose. Christ does not negotiate for the room; He calls it the guestchamber and sends word that He will eat there. That is the tone of an owner, and it belongs with the whole account of a Lord who knew the man with the pitcher of water before the disciples met him, who told them what would be said, and who went to the cross the next day exactly as He had said. The Supper was instituted by a Man in full command of the evening, which is why the Table He left is a memorial of a finished work and not of an accident.

pos: n. (a quarter of Jerusalem, the second district; where Huldah the prophetess dwelt — Hebrew mishneh)
etymology: Latin collegium, an association. The Hebrew mishneh means second — the second quarter of the city — and the margin of the Authorized Version offers both in the school and in the second part.
biblical_def: The college in the Authorized Version is a place in Jerusalem, and it is where the word of the LORD was sought at the most critical hour of Josiah's reign. The book of the law had been found in the house of the LORD, and when it was read the king rent his clothes and sent his highest officers with a commission: “Go ye, enquire of the LORD for me, and for the people, and for all Judah, concerning the words of this book that is found: for great is the wrath of the LORD that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not hearkened unto the words of this book” (2Ki 22:13). They went to a woman: “So Hilkiah the priest, and Ahikam, and Achbor, and Shaphan, and Asahiah, went unto Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tikvah, the son of Harhas, keeper of the wardrobe; (now she dwelt in Jerusalem in the college;) and they communed with her” (2Ki 22:14). The Chronicler records the same (2Ch 34:22). Huldah gave the word of the LORD plainly — judgment on the place, mercy on the king who had wept — and Josiah acted on it: “he read in their ears all the words of the book of the covenant which was found in the house of the LORD” (2Ki 23:2). The reformation of Judah began with a book found, a prophetess consulted in her own house, and a king who did what the book said.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a college as a collection or assembly; a society of persons engaged in common pursuits; and, in Scripture, the second quarter or district of Jerusalem.
webster_full: COL'LEGE, n. A collection or assembly; a society of men, invested with certain powers and rights.
2. An edifice appropriated to the use of students who are acquiring the languages and sciences.
3. In the Scriptures, a quarter or district of the city of Jerusalem; the margin reads, in the second part.
PROPH'ETESS, n. A female prophet; a woman who foretells future events, or who declares the word of God.
scriptures: 2 Kings 22:14

So Hilkiah the priest, and Ahikam, and Achbor, and Shaphan, and Asahiah, went unto Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tikvah, the son of Harhas, keeper of the wardrobe; (now she dwelt in Jerusalem in the college;) and they communed with her.
2 Kings 22:13

Go ye, enquire of the LORD for me, and for the people, and for all Judah, concerning the words of this book that is found: for great is the wrath of the LORD that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not hearkened unto the words of this book, to do according unto all that which is written concerning us.
2 Chronicles 34:22

And Hilkiah, and they that the king had appointed, went to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tikvath, the son of Hasrah, keeper of the wardrobe; (now she dwelt in Jerusalem in the college:) and they spake to her to that effect.
2 Kings 23:2

And the king went up into the house of the LORD, and all the men of Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem with him, and the priests, and the prophets, and all the people, both small and great: and he read in their ears all the words of the book of the covenant which was found in the house of the LORD.
corruption_summary: Huldah is pressed into service as a proof-text against the male eldership, and the passage's actual argument — that a nation was reformed by obeying a book — is passed over.
corruption_paragraphs: Huldah is regularly produced as evidence that Scripture's order of male eldership is a cultural residue. The narrative does not support the use. Huldah was a prophetess, and Scripture names several — Miriam, Deborah, Anna, the daughters of Philip — without ever appointing a woman to the office of elder or priest, which are the offices in question. The prophetic gift was never the pastoral office; Amos was a herdsman and Huldah a wife in the second quarter, and neither of them stood in the temple to minister. The same books that record her faithful word record the priesthood confined to the sons of Aaron, and the New Testament that records Philip's daughters prophesying also records the qualifications of an elder as the husband of one wife.

What the chapter is actually about deserves the attention the controversy takes from it. A copy of the law was found in a temple that had been running for years without it; when it was read the king tore his clothes; his officers sought a word from the LORD; the word came, plainly and without flattery, announcing judgment upon the place and mercy upon a king whose heart was tender; and Josiah then gathered the whole nation and read the book aloud to them, small and great. That is the pattern of every real reformation — the recovery of a text, grief at what it says, a plain word from God, and public obedience. The room where the word was sought is called the college, and no institution in it mattered half so much as the book they had lost.
roots_summary: Hebrew mishneh (H4932), second, the second district of the city — 2 Kings 22:14, 2 Chronicles 34:22, and Zephaniah 1:10 where it is rendered the second.

pos: n. (a raised road or ascent to the temple gate — Hebrew mesillah, a highway)
etymology: From Old French chaucie, a raised road, ultimately from Latin calx, limestone. The Hebrew mesillah is a built-up highway — a road raised above the ground it crosses.
biblical_def: The causeway was the raised ascent to the temple, and it appears in the assignment of the porters' wards under David: “To Shuppim and Hosah the lot came forth westward, with the gate Shallecheth, by the causeway of the going up, ward against ward” (1Ch 26:16), and “At Parbar westward, four at the causeway, and two at Parbar” (1Ch 26:18). The chapter is a duty roster. The porters were Levites, and their office was to keep the gates of the house of the LORD: “Among these were the divisions of the porters, even among the chief men, having wards one against another, to minister in the house of the LORD” (1Ch 26:12). Four gates, wards set opposite each other, lots cast for the stations, men posted on the raised road by which worshippers came up. The word mesillah is the same used by the prophet for a very different highway: “And an highway shall be there, and a way, and it shall be called The way of holiness; the unclean shall not pass over it; but it shall be for those: the wayfaring men, though fools, shall not err therein” (Isa 35:8). Israel's roads went up to the house of God, and its prophets used the road as the picture of the way to Him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a causey or causeway as a way raised above the natural level of the ground, by stones, earth or other materials, serving as a dry passage.
webster_full: CAUSEWAY, CAU'SEY, n. A way raised above the natural level of the ground, by stones, earth, timber, fascines, etc., serving as a dry passage over wet or marshy ground.
2. A paved way; a raised road.
POR'TER, n. A man that has the charge of a door or gate; a doorkeeper.
WARD, n. Guard; watch; a garrison; the act of guarding; a station or post of guard.
scriptures: 1 Chronicles 26:16
To Shuppim and Hosah the lot came forth westward, with the gate Shallecheth, by the causeway of the going up, ward against ward.
1 Chronicles 26:18
At Parbar westward, four at the causeway, and two at Parbar.
1 Chronicles 26:12
Among these were the divisions of the porters, even among the chief men, having wards one against another, to minister in the house of the LORD.
Isaiah 35:8

And an highway shall be there, and a way, and it shall be called The way of holiness; the unclean shall not pass over it; but it shall be for those: the wayfaring men, though fools, shall not err therein.
corruption_summary: The guarding of the door is despised as gatekeeping, and a house with no porters is called welcoming.
corruption_paragraphs: Chronicles takes a whole chapter to record who stood where at the gates of the house of God, and calls that standing a ministry: to minister in the house of the LORD. The office existed because a holy house has a threshold, and someone must know what may come in. The modern instinct treats every such office as exclusion for its own sake, and a church that has abolished its porters will find that it has not become more open but merely undefended. Guarding a door is not the opposite of welcoming people through it; the porters' whole business was to stand on the road by which worshippers came up.

Isaiah 35:8 shows what the raised road finally pictures, and it holds both truths at once. The way of holiness is closed — the unclean shall not pass over it — and it is astonishingly open: the wayfaring men, though fools, shall not err therein. A road so plain that a simple traveller cannot lose it, and so holy that the unclean cannot walk it. Only one thing reconciles those clauses, and it is the cleansing of the unclean, which is why the way is called by Him who said, I am the way, and no man cometh unto the Father but by me.

pos: n. (the prescribed formula of the holy oil and incense — Hebrew mathkoneth, a fixed proportion)
etymology: Latin compositio, a putting together. The Hebrew mathkoneth means a measured proportion or fixed formula — a recipe that may not be altered.
biblical_def: Composition in the Authorized Version means the exact prescribed formula of two holy things, and both times it appears God is forbidding imitation. Of the anointing oil: “Upon man's flesh shall it not be poured, neither shall ye make any other like it, after the composition of it: it is holy, and it shall be holy unto you” (Exo 30:32). Of the incense: “as for the perfume which thou shalt make, ye shall not make to yourselves according to the composition thereof: it shall be unto thee holy for the LORD” (Exo 30:37). The penalty is stated without qualification: “Whosoever compoundeth any like it, or whosoever putteth any of it upon a stranger, shall even be cut off from his people” (Exo 30:33). The oil itself was made by a specified art: “thou shalt make it an oil of holy ointment, an ointment compound after the art of the apothecary: it shall be an holy anointing oil” (Exo 30:25). Two principles are established. First, holy things are set apart by God's appointment, not by their ingredients — the same spices in another vessel are common. Second, God fixes the proportions of His own worship. Nothing here is left to the taste of the worshipper, and a man who improved on the formula was to be cut off.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines composition as the act of composing or putting together; the combination of ingredients in due proportion; a mixture or compound.
webster_full: COMPOSI'TION, n. In a general sense, the act of composing, or that which is composed; the act of forming a whole by uniting parts.
2. The combination of distinct substances or ingredients; a mixture or compound.
3. The proportion or arrangement of the parts of a mixture; as, the composition of an ointment.
APOTH'ECARY, n. One who practices pharmacy; one who prepares drugs and compounds medicines.
scriptures: Exodus 30:32
Upon man's flesh shall it not be poured, neither shall ye make any other like it, after the composition of it: it is holy, and it shall be holy unto you.
Exodus 30:37
And as for the perfume which thou shalt make, ye shall not make to yourselves according to the composition thereof: it shall be unto thee holy for the LORD.
Exodus 30:33
Whosoever compoundeth any like it, or whosoever putteth any of it upon a stranger, shall even be cut off from his people.
Exodus 30:25
And thou shalt make it an oil of holy ointment, an ointment compound after the art of the apothecary: it shall be an holy anointing oil.
corruption_summary: Worship is treated as an area of creative liberty, when Scripture fixes the composition of what God receives and cuts off the improver.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 30 is one of the plainest grounds of the regulative principle: what God has commanded in His worship is required, and what He has not commanded is not permitted. The oil and the incense were given by formula, and the man who reproduced them for other use was to be cut off from his people — not for wickedness in the ordinary sense, but for making a holy thing common. That is a severe doctrine and it is meant to be. It says that God fixes the terms on which He is approached, and that sincerity in the approacher settles nothing. Nadab and Abihu offered strange fire and died; Uzzah steadied the ark and died; the ground is the same.

The corresponding error is to conclude that God cares only about ceremony. He does not. The prophets pour scorn on incense offered by hands full of blood, and the same book that fixes the composition of the oil says obedience is better than sacrifice. Both stand. God appoints the manner of His worship, and God demands the heart of the worshipper, and a church that keeps the second while inventing freely in the first has claimed a liberty Exodus never granted. The apostolic rule for the New Testament assembly runs the same way: let all things be done decently and in order, and let all things be done unto edifying, by what Christ appointed and not by what pleases the congregation.

pos: n. pl. (the fruit of the olive; what is left after the shaking — Hebrew gargar)
etymology: Old English berie, a small fruit. In both scriptural uses the berries are olives — the Hebrew gargar is the olive berry left on the bough after the tree is beaten.
biblical_def: Berries in the Authorized Version are olives, and both occurrences are doctrinal. Isaiah describes what will be left of a nation under judgment: “Yet gleaning grapes shall be left in it, as the shaking of an olive tree, two or three berries in the top of the uppermost bough, four or five in the outmost fruitful branches thereof, saith the LORD God of Israel” (Isa 17:6). The picture is exact and it is a picture of the remnant. When an olive tree is beaten at harvest, a few berries always remain out of reach at the very top and on the far ends of the branches, and the poor came after and gleaned them by the law of God. So it will be with Israel: not a total end, but two or three in the top of the uppermost bough, left by God's own appointment. James uses the olive berry for a different point: “Can the fig tree, my brethren, bear olive berries? either a vine, figs? so can no fountain both yield salt water and fresh” (Jas 3:12), following his question, “Doth a fountain send forth at the same place sweet water and bitter?” (Jas 3:11). A tree bears after its kind, and a tongue speaks out of what a man is. Blessing God and cursing men out of the same mouth is a botanical impossibility dressed as religion.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a berry as a succulent or pulpy fruit containing naked seeds; and notes the scriptural use of the olive berry, the fruit of the olive tree.
webster_full: BER'RY, n. A succulent or pulpy fruit containing naked seeds.
2. In the Scriptures, the fruit of the olive tree; as, two or three berries in the top of the uppermost bough.
OL'IVE, n. A plant or tree of the genus Olea, of great value for its fruit and the oil expressed from it.
GLEAN, v.t. To gather the stalks and ears of grain, or the fruit left after the harvest.
scriptures: Isaiah 17:6

Yet gleaning grapes shall be left in it, as the shaking of an olive tree, two or three berries in the top of the uppermost bough, four or five in the outmost fruitful branches thereof, saith the LORD God of Israel.
James 3:12
Can the fig tree, my brethren, bear olive berries? either a vine, figs? so can no fountain both yield salt water and fresh.
James 3:11
Doth a fountain send forth at the same place sweet water and bitter?
Romans 11:17
And if some of the branches be broken off, and thou, being a wild olive tree, wert graffed in among them, and with them partakest of the root and fatness of the olive tree;
corruption_summary: Speech is treated as separable from character, so that a man may be judged by his convictions while his tongue is excused as temperament.
corruption_paragraphs: James 3 is built on the impossibility of a divided nature producing divided fruit, and the olive berry is his final illustration. A fig tree cannot bear olives; a fountain cannot give sweet and bitter at the same place. From which he concludes that a mouth which blesses God and curses men made in God's likeness is testifying against itself. The modern separation of a man's doctrine from his speech — sound convictions excusing a savage tongue, or a pleasant manner excusing false teaching — is precisely what James forbids. Both come out of the same root, and the root is what is actually being reported.

Isaiah's berries carry the doctrine of the remnant, and it must not be softened in either direction. The judgment is real: the tree is beaten, and what is left is two or three berries at the top. But the leaving is God's doing and it is stated by name — saith the LORD God of Israel. Paul takes up the same olive tree in Romans 11 to say that branches were broken off and a wild olive graffed in, and to warn the graffed branch not to boast against them. Where Gentile Christians read the remnant as Israel's failure rather than God's preservation, they take exactly the posture Paul forbids: thou bearest not the root, but the root thee.
