pos: n. pl. (goads; sharp points that drive a beast forward — Greek kentron)
etymology: Old English prica, a point. The Greek kentron is the ox-goad, a pointed stick used to drive cattle; the same word is used of the sting of death.
biblical_def: A prick is a goad, and the proverb the risen Christ quoted to Saul of Tarsus comes from the ploughed field: an ox that kicks back against the driver's pointed stick only drives it deeper into its own flesh. “And he said, Who art thou, Lord? And the Lord said, I am Jesus whom thou persecutest: it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks” (Act 9:5). Paul repeats it before Agrippa, adding that the voice spoke in the Hebrew tongue: “Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me? it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks” (Act 26:14), and “I said, Who art thou, Lord? And he said, I am Jesus whom thou persecutest” (Act 26:15). Two things are declared in that exchange. Christ identifies Himself with His people so completely that to touch them is to touch Him — He does not say my church, He says me. And the goad had been at work in Saul before the road: the memory of Stephen's face and Stephen's prayer, the arguments he could not answer, the conscience he was outrunning. Moses uses the word of a different goad: the nations left in the land “shall be pricks in your eyes, and thorns in your sides, and shall vex you in the land wherein ye dwell” (Num 33:55) — an unfinished obedience becomes a lifelong irritation.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a prick as a slender pointed instrument; a goad; and figuratively, a torment or painful reflection, as the pricks of conscience.
webster_full: PRICK, n. A slender pointed instrument or substance, which is hard enough to pierce the skin; a goad; a spur.
2. A puncture, or place entered by a point.
3. A painful thought or reflection; as the pricks of conscience.
GOAD, n. A pointed instrument used to stimulate a beast to move faster.
scriptures: Acts 9:5
And he said, Who art thou, Lord? And the Lord said, I am Jesus whom thou persecutest: it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks.
Acts 26:14
And when we were all fallen to the earth, I heard a voice speaking unto me, and saying in the Hebrew tongue, Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me? it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks.
Acts 26:15
And I said, Who art thou, Lord? And he said, I am Jesus whom thou persecutest.
Numbers 33:55

But if ye will not drive out the inhabitants of the land from before you; then it shall come to pass, that those which ye let remain of them shall be pricks in your eyes, and thorns in your sides, and shall vex you in the land wherein ye dwell.
corruption_summary: Conversion is presented as a decision a man reaches, when the Damascus road shows a man stopped, blinded, and told he has been kicking against a goad he did not choose.
corruption_paragraphs: Saul was not seeking Christ; he was riding to Damascus with letters to arrest Christians, and he was interrupted. The goad had been working — the Lord says as much — but the working of it had produced not repentance but harder kicking, and the persecution intensified rather than relented. That order of events is the standing refutation of every scheme in which the sinner initiates. Grace did not wait for Saul to soften; it knocked him to the ground on the road he had chosen, and the first word out of his mouth was a question because he had nothing prepared to say.

The Lord's wording is the second thing to hold. Why persecutest thou me? Saul had not laid a finger on Jesus of Nazareth; he had dragged men and women to prison. Christ counts it as done to Himself, and the union of Head and members is stated here more sharply than anywhere else in Acts. This is comfort to a persecuted church — no blow lands unfelt by Him — and it is a warning to anyone within the church who handles the saints roughly. Numbers 33:55 supplies the other lesson of the goad: what is not driven out will not lie quiet. An obedience left unfinished becomes the thing that pricks a man's eyes for the rest of his life in the land God gave him.

“I am Jesus whom thou persecutest” — not my church; me.
“Pricks in your eyes, and thorns in your sides” — what an unfinished obedience becomes.

pos: n. (a mark impressed; the mark of the nails in the risen body of Christ — Greek tupos)
etymology: Old French preinte, an impression, from Latin premere, to press. The Greek tupos means the mark left by a blow — and is the word from which type comes.
biblical_def: Print in the Authorized Version is a mark pressed into flesh, and its greatest use is Thomas's condition for believing: “The other disciples therefore said unto him, We have seen the Lord. But he said unto them, Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe” (Joh 20:25). Eight days later the Lord came and offered him exactly what he had demanded: “Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing” (Joh 20:27). The risen body of Christ carried the prints of the nails. He was raised incorruptible and glorious, and He kept the marks — the only work of man that survives into the resurrection. Job uses the word of God's close scrutiny: “thou puttest my feet also in the stocks, and lookest narrowly unto all my paths; thou settest a print upon the heels of my feet” (Job 13:27). And the law forbids a third kind: “Ye shall not make any cuttings in your flesh for the dead, nor print any marks upon you: I am the LORD” (Lev 19:28) — the body is not the mourner's to mark, because it is the LORD's.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a print as a mark made by impression; a stamp; the impression of any thing on another substance; that which is produced by pressure.
webster_full: PRINT, n. A mark made by impression; any line, character, figure or indentation made by the pressure of one body or thing on another.
2. The impressions of types in general, as to the form, size and face of the letter.
PRINT, v.t. To take an impression of; to mark by pressing one thing on another.
IM'PRESS, v.t. To imprint; to stamp; to fix deep.
scriptures: John 20:25

The other disciples therefore said unto him, We have seen the Lord. But he said unto them, Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe.
John 20:27
Then saith he to Thomas, Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing.
Leviticus 19:28
Ye shall not make any cuttings in your flesh for the dead, nor print any marks upon you: I am the LORD.
Thou puttest my feet also in the stocks, and lookest narrowly unto all my paths; thou settest a print upon the heels of my feet.
corruption_summary: The resurrection is spiritualized into a symbol or an inner experience, when the risen Christ offered a doubting man His hands and His side to handle.
corruption_paragraphs: Every account of the resurrection as a symbol of renewal, a survival of Jesus' influence, or an experience in the disciples' hearts is answered by one invitation: reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands. The Lord did not rebuke Thomas for wanting evidence; He supplied precisely the evidence demanded, and then called for faith. The body that rose was the body that died, identifiable by the prints of the nails, and Luke adds that He ate a piece of broiled fish before them. Christianity stands or falls on a fact of that order, and the church has no authority to convert it into a metaphor to keep it respectable.

The prints kept in the glorified body are worth a further thought. Everything else the world did to Christ was undone by the resurrection — the death, the shame, the grave. The nail marks were not. He carries into glory the evidence of what it cost to save His people, and John sees Him in heaven as a Lamb as it had been slain. Whatever else the doctrine of the resurrection body means, it does not mean the erasure of history. Leviticus 19:28 belongs here too: the marking of the body was forbidden because the body is the LORD's and the pagan mourning rites treated it otherwise; the only marks Scripture honours are the ones Christ bore, and the ones Paul said he bore in his body for Christ's sake.
roots_summary: Greek tupos (G5179), the mark of a blow, an impression, a type — John 20:25; Hebrew qaaqa (H7085), an incision or imprinted mark, Leviticus 19:28 only; chaqah (H2707), to carve or set a print.
roots_lines: Greek tupos (G5179) — the print of a blow, a stamp, a pattern; John 20:25, and Romans 5:14 where Adam is the figure of Him that was to come.
Hebrew qaaqa (H7085) — an imprinted mark or tattoo; Leviticus 19:28, its only occurrence.
Hebrew chaqah (H2707) — to carve, cut in, set a print; Job 13:27, Ezekiel 23:14.
The same Greek word gives us type: a mark pressed in, and a pattern pressed out.
Revelation 5:6 sees Him in the midst of the throne as a Lamb as it had been slain — the marks are kept.
usage: “Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails” — and He offered exactly that.
“Be not faithless, but believing” — the evidence given, then the call to faith.
“Nor print any marks upon you: I am the LORD” — the body is not the mourner's to mark.

pos: n. (two of a kind reckoned together; in Scripture, of shoes, turtledoves and balances — Greek zugos)
etymology: Latin par, equal, through Old French paire. The Greek zugos in Revelation 6:5 is a yoke or beam — a pair of balances is a yoke with a scale hung at either end.
biblical_def: Pair is a small word, and Scripture uses it at three heavy moments. Amos twice indicts Israel for the price at which men were sold: “because they sold the righteous for silver, and the poor for a pair of shoes” (Amo 2:6), and “That we may buy the poor for silver, and the needy for a pair of shoes; yea, and sell the refuse of the wheat?” (Amo 8:6). A man's freedom bartered for footwear — the prophet names the exchange rate to expose the contempt. Luke records the offering brought for the infant Christ: “And to offer a sacrifice according to that which is said in the law of the Lord, A pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons” (Luk 2:24). That was the concession Leviticus made for those who could not afford a lamb, and it tells us the household into which the Son of God was born. Revelation puts the word in the hand of the third horseman: “lo a black horse; and he that sat on him had a pair of balances in his hand” (Rev 6:5), and the voice that follows prices wheat and barley at famine rates. The three uses hold together: the poor sold for a pair of shoes, the Saviour's mother offering the poor woman's pair of birds, and a pair of balances weighing out bread in judgment.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a pair as two things of a kind, similar in form, applied to like things used together; two of a sort; a couple.
webster_full: PAIR, n. Two things of a kind, similar in form, applied to the same purpose, or suited to each other; as a pair of shoes, a pair of gloves.
2. Two of a sort; a couple; a brace; as a pair of turtledoves.
3. In arithmetic and commerce, two corresponding parts of an instrument; as a pair of balances.
BAL'ANCE, n. A pair of scales for weighing commodities; a beam suspended in the middle, with a scale at each end.
scriptures: Revelation 6:5
And when he had opened the third seal, I heard the third beast say, Come and see. And I beheld, and lo a black horse; and he that sat on him had a pair of balances in his hand.
Luke 2:24
And to offer a sacrifice according to that which is said in the law of the Lord, A pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.
Amos 2:6
Thus saith the LORD; For three transgressions of Israel, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because they sold the righteous for silver, and the poor for a pair of shoes;
Amos 8:6
That we may buy the poor for silver, and the needy for a pair of shoes; yea, and sell the refuse of the wheat?
corruption_summary: Poverty is treated as evidence of God's displeasure, when the law made a poor man's offering acceptable and the Lord of glory was presented with it.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 2:24 settles a great deal by a small detail. Leviticus 12 required a lamb for a burnt offering and a young pigeon for a sin offering, and then made a provision: if she be not able to bring a lamb, then she shall bring two turtles or two young pigeons. Mary brought the pair of birds. The mother of the Lord came under the poverty clause of the law, and the offering was received without the smallest hint of deficiency. That is the standing answer to every doctrine that reads wealth as favour and want as judgment, and it is the answer God gave first by arranging the circumstances of His own Son's infancy.

Amos supplies the other half. God did not overlook what was being done to the poor of Israel, and the phrase He fastened on was the price: the poor for a pair of shoes. What the prophet exposes is not merely injustice but contempt — men bartered as cheaply as footwear, and the refuse of the wheat sold to them afterward. Wherever a system prices human beings so, Amos 2:6 is the verdict already pronounced. And the third seal keeps the accounting: a pair of balances in the hand of the rider, weighing out a day's wage for a day's wheat, so that men who dealt in false balances are finally weighed in a true one.
roots_summary: Greek zeugos (G2201), a yoke, a pair — Luke 2:24, Luke 14:19; zugos (G2218), a yoke or beam of a balance — Revelation 6:5; Hebrew naal (H5275), a sandal or pair of shoes.
roots_lines: Greek zeugos (G2201) — a pair, a yoke of animals; Luke 2:24 of the turtledoves, Luke 14:19 of five yoke of oxen.
Greek zugos (G2218) — a yoke, and the beam of a balance; Revelation 6:5, Matthew 11:29 of His easy yoke.
Hebrew naal (H5275) — a sandal; Amos 2:6 and 8:6, the price at which the poor were sold.
Leviticus 12:8 makes the pair of birds the offering of the woman who cannot afford a lamb.
Proverbs 11:1 sets the standard the third seal enforces: a false balance is abomination to the LORD.
usage: “The poor for a pair of shoes” — the prophet names the exchange rate.
“A pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons” — the poor woman's offering, brought for Christ.
“A pair of balances in his hand” — false weights answered by a true one.
